title: Insight
hookLine: seeing impermanence, unsatisfactoriness and not-self in your own experience

lines: THE HARDEST THING, OR EVERYTHING CHANGED.
cards: You've probably seen a sign for it: a ten-day silent retreat. No phones, no talking, no eye contact, up before dawn, meditating most of the day. People come back and struggle to describe what happened.
Some say it was the hardest thing they've ever done. Some say it changed how they see everything. The courses have spread from Myanmar and India to many countries.
The word on the sign is a Pali one, and it names the second wing of yesterday's bird. Today: insight.

teach.b: Vipassanā. Passanā means seeing; the vi in front is usually read as clearly, or through. Seeing clearly.
Seeing through. What does insight see?
The Theravada tradition says: three marks that belong to everything that's put together. Anicca: it changes. Dukkha: because it changes, it can't finally satisfy.
Anattā: there's no fixed self inside it that owns it. You've heard these before on this path. Insight is the difference between hearing them and seeing them in your own experience.
The Dhammapada puts the first mark this way, in Max Müller's English: "'All created things perish,' he who knows and sees this becomes passive in pain; this is the way to purity."
Passive in pain is Müller's old phrasing for growing weary of what causes suffering, letting go. The next two verses say the same about the other marks. Notice the verb: knows and sees.

Not believes. Insight practice turns attention on the moment-to-moment stream of body and mind: an itch that arises, peaks and fades; a thought that seems solid, then dissolves; a mood you'd sworn was you, gone by lunch.
Seen over and over, the tradition says, the grip loosens by itself.
In modern times, Burmese teachers brought this practice out of the monasteries to lay people. The monk Ledi Sayadaw was among the early ones. A layman, U Ba Khin, taught S.
N. Goenka, who took ten-day courses to the world. Tomorrow, another Burmese method.
Today, the tradition's own instruction: don't take it on trust.

how: Vipassana is taught in Theravada monasteries and in lay meditation centers worldwide, often in silent retreats of ten days or more; S. N. Goenka's courses and the Mahasi centers are two widely known lines of teaching.

o: seeing change and not-self in your own experience
a relaxing technique for easing everyday stress
trusting the teachings without testing them

games.q: during a sit, an itch appears on your nose. you're practicing insight. what do you do?
o: watch it arise, peak and change, and see what happens.
decide it means you're doing it wrong.
games.why: insight practice turns attention to how each sensation changes; seen closely, even an itch shows the first mark.

practice: Pick any sensation, the touch of your hands, the air at the nose, a small ache, and watch it closely: does it stay exactly the same, or does it shift, pulse, fade, return? When a sound or a thought comes, notice it begin and end.
Nothing to fix; just see each thing change.

wordCard.voice: Vipassana. Insight: seeing change, unsatisfactoriness and not-self in your own experience, not just believing them.

orig.note: Pali vipassanā: insight, clear seeing; Sanskrit vipaśyanā.

carryVoice: Your line: see clearly. Even a strong mood can be watched like weather, arriving, changing, going. See you tomorrow.
